news_title: Pressure rising on Karnataka government to withdraw anti-cow slaughter and anti-conversion laws
efet_title: Pressure rising on Karnataka government to withdraw anti-cow slaughter and anti-conversion laws
efet_body:
Pressure rising on Karnataka government to withdraw anti-cow slaughter and anti-conversion laws
Updated
- October 06, 2026 12:09 pm IST - Bengaluru
Sharath S. Srivatsa
READ LATER
SEE ALL
Remove
A file photo of a protest rally against the anti-conversion Bill, which was tabled during the Winter Session of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly, in Bengaluru in December 2021.
| Photo Credit: File photo
The Congress government seems to be under pressure as restive Muslim and Christian communities have come together with a demand to act on the party’s promise to withdraw the Karnataka Prevention of Slaughter and Preservation of Cattle Act, 2020, popularly known as the anti-cow slaughter legislation, and the Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act, 2022, known as the anti-conversion Act.
Besides, Muslims are seeking clarity on the government’s stand over reservation for them under 2B category, and are urging the government to increase the reservation from 4% to 8% based on the population. Christians are demanding a separate 1% reservation under the OBC reservation matrix. The communities have also sought clarity on the imbroglio over the hate speech Bill.
Though former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah had initiated the process to withdraw/amend the legislations in the initial days of the second tenure in 2023, it came under pressure from Hindu mutt seers, who had collectively opposed any such move, forcing the government to backtrack.
While the respective community leaders have met Congress’s legislators and senior leadership separately on multiple occasions to press for their demands, the community leaders are also planning a coordinated effort ahead of the Winter Session in December. “We have waited over three years for the government to act. The community has become restive at the inaction. What is the difference between the Congress and BJP governments, if it continues with the same legislations? Muslims suffered under the BJP and incidents of attack on Christians continue even now,” said Shabeer Ahmed, Karnataka Rajya Muslim Okkoota (KRMO) Steering Committee member. “The Winter Session would be the last possible window for the government to withdraw the legislation, and two communities are working together.”
In May, after the KRMO announced a muslim convention where “Promises of Congress Government, Gaps in Delivery and Charter of Demands” was released, the State government withdrew the contentious ban on Muslim girls wearing hijab to educational institutions as a damage control measure. The Congress government, however, viewed the convention as embarrassing and that damaged the party’s image. In a controversial move, the BJP government in 2022 had banned wearing the hijab in educational institutions.
“Both communities are coming together in a big way across the State. Jointly strategies have been drawn for certain programmes to create awareness within communities and to take our demand to a logical end. Plans are afoot to hold a massive joint protest in November. Joint protests will also be held in district centres,” acknowledged J.A. Kanthraj, spokesperson of the Archdiocese of Bangalore.
One of the Cabinet Ministers said that the government could move on the two legislations since the Congress has attained majority in the Upper House only recently. Stating that the government was still “mulling over” the legislations, another senior Minister said that the government would abide by the Supreme Court ruling on hate speech in which the apex court said that the current provisions were adequate to address hate speech. Incidentally, the Ministry of Home Affairs stalled the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, passed by both Houses of the legislature, citing that the provisions of BNS was adequate, after the Karnataka Governor referred the Bill to the President.
Asked if there was any pressure against action on the anti-cow slaughter and anti-conversion laws, the Minister said: “There is no pressure on us. The Law Department will take a call on it.”
When his views were sought, Minister for Health and Family Welfare, Minority Affairs, Haj and Wakf U.T. Khader said: “There is a demand to do it. The government (under Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar) is new. It is aware of the issue and is positively thinking about it.”

news_title: FSSAI issues order to intensify food safety crackdown across India ahead of festive season to prevent sale of ‘adulterated, unsafe products’
efet_title: FSSAI issues order to intensify food safety crackdown across India ahead of festive season to prevent sale of ‘adulterated, unsafe products’
efet_body:
FSSAI issues order to intensify food safety crackdown across India ahead of festive season to prevent sale of ‘adulterated, unsafe products’
The order calls for the strategic deployment of Food Safety on Wheels (FSWs), a functional mobile laboratory for food testing, in prominent markets.
Updated on: Oct 6, 2026, 14:24:27 IST
By
Stuti Gupta
Prefer HT
on Google
Share via
Copy link
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had issued a directive to food safety authorities across all states and union territories to step up surveillance and enforcement actions against unsafe food products in light of the upcoming festive season.
The festive season typically brings a spike in demand for multiple food items such as milk and milk products, sweets, snacks and savouries including Namkeen, papad/fryums, edible oil, beverages, ghee, etc. (PTI/ Representational)
The festive season typically brings a spike in demand for multiple food items such as dairy products, sweets, snacks and savouries including Namkeen, papad/fryums, edible oil, beverages, ghee, etc.
FSSAI calls for heightened surveillance, strict action
As per the directive, heightened inspection and enforcement actions are meant to prevent the circulation of “adulterated, counterfeited and unsafe food products”. Beyond the food items mentioned, the FSSAI also asks regional agencies to expand the list of targeted commodities as per local eating and consumption patterns.
In order to address this public health concern, all enforcement officials (Designated Officers/ Food Safety Officers/ Central Food Safety Officers), under the directives of their respective commissioners, will be deployed to conduct inspection and sampling in their respective regions during the festive period. As per judgement, food hot spots and other sensitive locations are to come under special focus in this matter.
In addition, the order calls for the strategic deployment of Food Safety on Wheels (FSWs), a functional mobile laboratory for food testing, in prominent market areas. Based on intel received, the initiative is meant to push for on-spot-testing of food safety norms, strengthening hygiene vigilance and boosting consumer confidence during a period of flooded demand in the market.
All relevant data in lieu with inspection, sampling, and outcome must mandatorily be uploaded or recorded on FoSCoS/FoSCoRIS on a real-time basis, the notice further states.
Also Read I
FSSAI suspends Seven Seas Hospitality licence over foul odour, fungal growth, filth
Recent crackdowns to ensure safety compliance
The FSSAI has, in recent times, cracked down on multiple eateries and products to ensure compliance with food safety norms. The body recently banned the sale of
Nestle's “Low Fat Dairy Whitener”
after a sample of the product taken from The Lalit hotel in New Delhi's Connaught Place was declared to be “unsafe” and “substandard”.
FSSAI gave the company an opportunity to appeal against the Food Analyst's report under the FSS Act, 2006, within a prescribed time period. Nestle, however, claimed that the product was safe to consume and compliant will all applicable regulatory requirements.
A
food vending unit was shut down
in Govindpura, Manimajra last Thursday after the health department found the vendor running the business in unhygienic conditions, without registering with the FSSAI.
The official of the food safety administration revealed that the kitchen of the vendor concerned was found dirty, with food not stored properly and kept in open, walls not being properly painted, workers in shabby clothes, dirty utensils, and unhygienic washing area.
Hence, the order ahead of the festive season is the latest directive in a series of crackdowns by the food safety regulatory body to enforce compliance with safety norms.

Bihar police job aspirants march in Patna, seek withdrawal of exam cancellation
The Bihar Police Subordinate Services Commission (BPSSC) had cancelled the examination on September 23 for recruitment to 1,799 posts.
Published on: Oct 5, 2026, 14:49:23 IST
PTI

on Google

Job aspirants held a protest march in Patna on Monday, demanding withdrawal of the cancellation of the sub-inspector mains examination.
The aspirants, who had cleared the examinations, began their march from Gandhi Maidan towards the chief minister's residence. (PTI)
The Bihar Police Subordinate Services Commission (BPSSC) had cancelled the examination on September 23 for recruitment to 1,799 posts, citing "unavoidable reasons".
The aspirants, who had cleared the examinations, began their march from Gandhi Maidan towards the chief minister's residence but were stopped by police at JP Golambar.

"We passed the preliminary and mains examinations, and were preparing for the physical test. However, the examination was abruptly cancelled. No concrete reason was provided," a protester, Raunak Kumar, told PTI Videos.
"Our demand is that the recruitment process be resumed immediately and dates for the physical examination be announced," he said.
Also Read |

Kumar alleged that the government had "succumbed to pressure politics" by a "handful of unsuccessful candidates".
Another protester, Nidhi, said candidates like her had "invested more than a year to prepare for the examination" and wanted to meet Chief Minister Samrat Chaudhary to convey their concerns.

The cancellation followed a protest by another group of job aspirants in Patna last month, who alleged irregularities in the examination.

efet_body:

FSSAI steps up action against brands over unsafe products, misleading claims: Do consumers need simpler food labels?
FSSAI has stepped up scrutiny of major food brands over unsafe products and misleading claims. Nutritionists say consumers need clearer, more transparent labels that help them identify key nutritional information without being swayed by marketing claims.
Swati Gandhi
Published
6 Oct 2026, 09:05 AM IST
Prefer Livemint
on Google
FSSAI has stepped up scrutiny of major food brands over unsafe products and misleading claims. | AI-generated image for representational purposes only
(
AI-generated image
)
AI Quick Read
From recalling an Everest cumin powder over unsafe pesticide levels to action against Dabur's "100 per cent" claims and proceedings against Nestlé over infant nutrition products and a dairy whitener sample, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (
FSSAI
) is stepping up its scrutiny of some of the country's biggest food and beverage brands.
Also Read
|
FSSAI recalls Everest cumin powder from market: Here's why
FSSAI's recent crackdown against brands
Earlier in September, the FSSAI stepped up its regulatory scrutiny of FMCG major
Dabur
and called for a statutory audit covering 27 product lines. The action covered several consumer categories, including homemade brands, glucose powders and high-margin direct-to-consumer (D2C) wellness products. The food safety regulator also raised concerns over claims suggesting medicinal benefits for products such as cold-pressed oils, apple cider vinegar and honey, and directed the company to remove or withdraw such claims.
Previously, Dabur India was also barred from selling food products that carried claims such as "100% Pure", "100% Natural", "100% Purity Guaranteed", "100% Organic" and "100% Tender Coconut Water".
In a separate incident, the FSSAI ordered an immediate ban on the sale of Nestlé's Low Fat
Dairy Whitener
after a sample collected from The Lalit Hotel in New Delhi was found to be "unsafe" and "substandard".
On 4 October, the food safety regulator also asked
Everest
Food Products to recall its 'pre-packed cumin powder' from the market after a sample was found unsafe for consumption.
Also Read
|
Are Food MNCs Treating India Like A 3rd World Market?
These recent actions raise a broader question for consumers: Do Indians need simpler food labels to understand what they are actually buying? Should consumers have to rely on FSSAI action to flag misleading claims, or should food labels be simple and transparent enough for them to make informed choices themselves?
Experts advocate for simpler food labels
Saloni, a nutritionist and founder of Femly, told
LiveMint
that Indians need simpler, more consumer-friendly food labels. "Today, a lot of the information on a package is technically correct, but that doesn't necessarily mean it is easy for the average person to understand," she said.
Elaborating, she said, "When you're standing in a supermarket, you shouldn't need to be a nutritionist to figure out what you're buying. Consumers should be able to look at a packet and quickly understand the basics: what are the main ingredients, how much sugar, sodium and saturated fat does it contain."
According to Sonal Nakra, Consultant Nutritionist & Founder, Eat and Heal, India needs "honest" labels rather than those that are just "simple". She said the country is sitting on a metabolic health time bomb, home to over 100 million people living with
diabetes
and millions more suffering from premature hypertension.
When asked whether Indians should be worried about complex terms on the backs of products, the two experts explained that they shouldn't be worried, but they must be informed. According to Saloni, a complicated ingredient name does not automatically mean an ingredient is harmful. Many ingredients have scientific names because they perform a specific function in food.
Also Read
|
FSSAI action at Seven Seas: What did the food regulator find?
Echoing Saloni's sentiment, Nakra suggested a few ways to navigate labelling without falling into scaremongering.
Natural doesn't always mean safe:
"Natural" or "herbal" does not automatically mean chemical-free or safer than synthetic ingredients.
Dose matters:
The risk of an additive depends on how much is consumed, so consumers should consider portion size and overall nutrition.
Sugar can hide behind different names:
Ingredients such as maltodextrin, dextrose, rice syrup and invert sugar can make it harder to identify total sugar intake.
When asked which terms consumers should be most cautious about, the experts suggested looking beyond front-of-pack claims such as "Multigrain", "Natural" or "No Added Sugar". Additionally, they should pay special attention to added sugar, sodium, saturated fat, and trans fat, and review the overall ingredient list. These are more meaningful things to monitor than simply looking for ingredients with unfamiliar names, they said.

FSSAI recalls popular brand’s cumin powder after sample found unsafe: Check the batch number and learn how to spot adulterated cumin seeds and powder at home
TIMESOFINDIA.COM /

Save

1

FSSAI: M/s Everest Food Products Private Limited has been directed to immediately recall "Pre-packed Cumin Powder" after tests declared the sample "UNSAFE".
One batch of a popular cumin powder has now been pulled into a food-safety investigation after a laboratory sample was declared “UNSAFE”. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has ordered an immediate recall of the implicated batch of Everest pre-packed cumin powder after testing found two pesticide residues above the prescribed maximum limits.
The recall raises a more everyday question for consumers: what should genuine cumin look like, and can adulteration be spotted at home?
2
/
5
Why FSSAI recalled the cumin powder
According to FSSAI, a regulatory sample of pre-packed cumin powder was collected from the premises of Riverside Resorts & Holiday Homes Pvt Ltd in Goa.
The Food Analyst detected residues of Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam at levels exceeding the prescribed maximum limits. The sample was consequently declared “UNSAFE” under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The batch number identified in the recall is E080668761. FSSAI also directed the company to maintain records of the recalled product, submit the required recall information and take corrective measures to prevent a recurrence.
3
/
5
Cumin powder is easier to adulterate
There is another reason consumers often find it difficult to judge powdered spices.
FSSAI has pointed out that spices sold in ground form can be easier to adulterate because consumers cannot easily see what went into the powder. Its food-safety material lists several substances that may be mixed into ground spices, including cheaper materials such as flour, starch, sawdust and chalk powder.
For cumin specifically, FSSAI has identified coloured grass seeds and fennel seeds among possible adulterants.
That is where whole cumin seeds offer one simple advantage: you can actually look at them.
4
/
5
How to check cumin seeds at home
FSSAI's consumer-awareness material includes simple household tests for common adulterants.
For cumin seeds, one test involves rubbing the seeds between your palms. If the palms turn black, FSSAI says it indicates possible adulteration with grass seeds coloured with charcoal dust.
Another FSSAI DART test is specifically designed to detect fennel seeds mixed with cumin. The recommended method is visual: place a small quantity of cumin seeds on a glass plate and examine them closely. Fennel seeds can be separated by careful observation.
For powdered spices, FSSAI also provides rapid household tests through its Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test (DART) programme. The regulator says its DART booklet contains more than 50 tests covering different food products and common adulterants.
But a home test is only a quick screening method. It cannot establish whether a packaged product contains pesticide residues or whether a particular chemical is above its legally permitted limit. Such findings require laboratory testing.
5
/
5
What consumers should check now
The immediate point for anyone who has the recalled product at home is simple: check the batch number before using it. If it is E080668761, it is the batch covered by the FSSAI recall.
FSSAI maintains a public food-recall system so consumers can check information about unsafe or non-compliant food products withdrawn from the market.
And the larger lesson goes beyond one packet of cumin. A spice can look, smell and taste normal and still require laboratory testing to establish whether it meets food-safety standards. For consumers, buying properly labelled products, checking recall information and knowing the basic visual signs of adulteration can add one more layer of protection in the kitchen.

In a social media post on Sunday, FSSAI said it continues to enforce strict regulatory compliance to safeguard consumer health across the country.
"FSSAI licence of Creative Bakers and Confectioners Pvt Ltd has been suspended with immediate effect due to severe hygiene deficiencies," it said.
Moreover, the FSSAI has issued a product recall order against Everest Food Products Pvt Ltd.
Advt
The regulator has directed Everest Food to "immediately recall 'Pre-packed Cumin Powder' after tests declared the sample unsafe".
A regulatory sample of "Pre-packed Cumin Powder" was drawn from the premises of Riverside Resorts & Holiday Homes Pvt Ltd, Goa.
"The Food Analyst's report found pesticide residues of Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam at levels exceeding the prescribed maximum limits," it said.
The food analyst declared the sample "UNSAFE" under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The company was provided an opportunity to appeal against the report, following which the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory.
The referral lab confirmed that the sample was "UNSAFE" as Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam were found above the prescribed maximum limits.
The entire implicated batch of "Pre-packed Cumin Powder" was directed to be recalled immediately from the market.
Everest Food was directed to maintain complete records of the recalled product and submit the reports.
"The FBO was further directed to undertake corrective measures to prevent recurrence of the incident and submit a report upon completion of the recall," the regulator said.
In the past few months, FSSAI has stepped up enforcement action against food business operators and e-commerce companies. It is informing the public at large about these actions through social media.

efet_body:
FSSAI recalls Everest cumin power over ‘unsafe’ pesticide levels, suspends Creative Bakers' licence
The FSSAI has, over the past six months, stepped up enforcement actions and relays them to food business operators and the public through social media.
Updated on: Oct 4, 2026, 17:53:23 IST
Edited by
Arya Mishra
Prefer HT
on Google
Share via
Copy link
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India on Sunday ordered immediate recall of a batch of Everest pre-packed cumin powder after a regulatory sample was found to contain pesticide residues above prescribed limits and declared “unsafe.”
The Food Analyst's report of the Everest cumin powder was found to have pesticide residues above maximum limits. (X/ @fssaiindia)
In a separate action, the regulator also suspended the licence of Creative Bakers and Confectioners Pvt Ltd – which operates the retail chain The Sugarr & Spice across several outlets in Eastern India – with immediate effect over serious hygiene, sanitation and food safety violations.
The FSSAI has, over the past six months, stepped up enforcement actions, and relays them to the food business operators and the public through its official handles on social media platforms.
ALSO READ:
Nestle's dairy whitener collected from top Delhi hotel found to be 'unsafe', FSSAI bans sale
‘Pesticide residues exceeding maximum limits’: FSSAI on Everest cumin powder recall
In a notification on Sunday, the FSSAI said a regulatory sample of Everest's “pre-packed cumin powder” was drawn from the premises of M/s Riverside Resorts & Holiday Homes Pvt. Ltd., Goa. The Food Analyst's report of this sample found the product to have pesticide residues of Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam at levels exceeding the prescribed maximum limit, it said.
"The Food Analyst declared the sample "UNSAFE" under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006," the FSSAI said. It added that the food business operator (FBO), in this case Everest, was provided an opportunity to appeal against the report, following which the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory.
"The Referral Food Laboratory confirmed that the sample was "UNSAFE", as Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam were found above the prescribed maximum limits," the food safety regulator stated. Following this, the entire batch of the product was directed to be recalled immediately from the market, and Everest was ordered to “maintain complete records of the recalled product and submit the prescribed recall information and status reports within the stipulated timelines.”
“The FBO was further directed to undertake corrective measures to prevent recurrence of the incident and submit a report upon completion of the recall,”
FSSAI
added.
Also Read | FSSAI suspends licence of Delhi-based hospitality establishment for ‘serious non-compliance’
‘Dirt, grease, dust, cobwebs’: Why FSSAI suspended Creative Bakers' licence
In its notification about the suspension of licence of Creative Bakers and Confectioners Pvt Ltd, the FSSAI flagged “severe hygiene and sanitation deficiencies”, including “dirt, grease, dust, cobwebs and flies in food production and handling areas.”
The regulator said it found perishable raw materials being stored “openly”, adding that rusted and inadequately cleaned containers were being used for raw and semi-finished products. “Significant pest infestation and inadequate pest-control measures were observed, including ineffective fly control, absence of proper rodent control and openings/windows without insect-proof mesh,” FSSAI added.
It said that waste, old stock, rejected lots and scrap were found to be accumulated in the food handling areas of the confectioner's premises, while rusting equipment, flaking paint, dampness and broken floor tiles were also observed. “Required food safety records and systems, including water and finished-product testing, time-temperature monitoring, calibration, preventive maintenance, mock recall, consumer complaints, straining and audit records, were not properly maintained,” the regulator added. The FBO was then directed to cease all food business activities during the suspension period, FSSAI said.

NEW DELHI: A sample of Nestlé India’s Low Fat Dairy Whitener, collected from the premises of The LaLiT in Connaught Place, has been declared “unsafe and substandard” by a Food Analyst’s laboratory, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Saturday.
The sample was collected from M/s Bharat Hotels Ltd (The LaLiT), Connaught Place, FSSAI said. The regulator said the Food Analyst’s report found the product non-compliant under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
FSSAI said a copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator and a notice was issued regarding the non-compliant product. The operator was given an opportunity to appeal against the Food Analyst’s report within the prescribed period.
FSSAI also directed that the identified product be immediately prohibited from sale.
However, Nestlé India said the product is safe to consume and complies with all applicable regulatory requirements.
A Nestlé India spokesperson said phosphorus occurs naturally in milk and is therefore present in milk-based products. The company said the FSSAI laboratory report reflects total phosphorus against the additive limit without accounting for the substantial natural phosphorus contribution from milk-based ingredients.
Nestlé said the product is in full compliance with prescribed limits for added phosphorus under the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, including on an “as consumed” basis. The company said it has been engaging with the authorities through the due process established under law and has shared data on other same or similar milk-based products to demonstrate the presence of naturally occurring phosphorus.

The hotel said it simultaneously discontinued use of the product and removed all packets from its operations.
“The matter concerning the product’s compliance is between FSSAI and Nestlé India and not with The LaLiT,” Shukla said, adding that the hotel had acted promptly after receiving the communication and remained committed to food safety protocols and compliance with FSSAI regulations.

A man who left his family and a stable job in India to relocate to Canada recalled the hurdles he faced on his way to success. He shared how, after moving abroad, he worked 12-hour night shifts for $16 an hour at a fast-food chain.
The NRI who now lives in Canada. (LinkedIn/Kamal Nanda)
The
video
the NRI, Kamal Nanda, shared shows a split screen along with text inserts. The first one reads, “2023: I left my family and a stable job in India to flip burgers 12 hours a night for $16 an hour.”

The text on the second part of the screen reads, “2026: I work from home with real work-life balance and travel in Canada for work.”
“A drunk
customer
threw a drink at me over a five-minute wait. We were short-staffed. They yelled, cursed, and threw it anyway,” the Canada-based entrepreneur wrote on Instagram.
He recalled that was the day he decided that he didn’t relocate to another country to be treated like that. Determined to change his future, he started “applying for jobs vigorously.” Not just applying for jobs before shifts, he even took one interview mid-shift, during lunch break.
What happened next?
Nanda recalled, “It turned into a freelance project. No payroll. No guarantee. I took it anyway and kept the burger job part-time.”
He continued, “For almost seven months, my days looked like this: 9 to 5 at my new job. An hour’s drive to the burger job. 6 to 11. Sometimes midnight. 30 minutes home. Eat. Sleep. Repeat. Then the freelance turned full-time. I left the fast food chain for good.”
The man shared that his professional journey wasn’t a “straight line after that”, adding, “I left for a new opportunity, and two months in, they let me go. The next 30 days were tough. In those 30 days, I got 10 interviews and 3 offers. What made the difference: The urge to get out. Upskilling every day. Taking a chance on something that wasn’t stable.”
Advising those who are in a situation like he was, he shared, “Look at yourself in the mirror. Be honest about where you’re lacking. Your resume. Reaching out. Networking. Applying to the right roles for your skillset. You’re busy. I get that. However, find one or two hours anyway.”
He added, “Be patient. It takes time. Keep working on yourself.”

efet_body:
View Market Dashboard
‘Do not disappoint us’: SC reserves order on FSSAI front-of-pack labels
The Supreme Court asked FSSAI to implement front-of-pack warning labels on packaged foods in the ‘true spirit’ and within the prescribed timeline. The regulator has proposed a single-phase system with red-hexagon warnings for products exceeding sugar, salt, fat and other nutrient thresholds.
Krishna Yadav
Updated
28 Sep 2026, 02:20 PM IST
Prefer Livemint
on Google
The top court also took on record an affidavit filed by the FSSAI setting out the regulator’s latest position on the proposed warning-label regime.
(
ANI
)
AI Quick Read
The Supreme Court on Monday told the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to implement its final directions on front-of-the-pack warning labels in their “true spirit” and within the prescribed timeline, asking the regulator not to disappoint the court.
“On the day when the matter comes up for reporting compliance, do not disappoint us. We expect the authority to comply [with] each and everything in the larger interest of the nation,” the two-judge bench said while concluding the hearing on a petition seeking mandatory warning labels on packaged food products.
However, the bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran reserved its order for final directions.
The court heard arguments on several aspects of the proposed labelling framework, including added sugar, nutrient thresholds, voluntary compliance, treatment of existing stocks and the timeline for implementation.
The top court also took on record an affidavit filed by the
FSSAI
setting out the regulator’s latest position on the proposed warning-label regime.
The FSSAI has proposed moving away from its earlier two-phase implementation approach and adopting a single-phase system for front-of-the-pack warning labels. Under the proposed framework, a packaged food product could be required to carry a warning if even one of the specified nutrients crosses the prescribed threshold.
The regulator has proposed a red hexagon placed on a white square background at the top-left of the package, intended to provide
consumers
with a prominent visual indication when a packaged food product exceeds the prescribed limits for nutrients of concern.
Also Read
|
Industry has to follow the consumer, says FSSAI chief on food-safety push
The SC had earlier asked the regulator to clarify 13 issues relating to the proposed warning system, including the timeline for implementation, the basis for the two-phase approach, treatment of sweetened beverages, processing levels, sugar and fat calculations, the colour and design of warnings, pictorial representations, additives, voluntary compliance and nutrition literacy.
Health warning
Non-profit 3S and Our Health Society filed a public interest litigation (PIL) seeking stronger front-of-the-pack warnings on packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat in August 2024.
The FSSAI sought about four months to finalize the regulations, followed by a proposed 365-day voluntary compliance period for food businesses.
During Monday’s hearing, the court questioned the time being sought by the FSSAI to implement the proposed framework. The regulator has indicated that it would need time to draft and finalize the regulations, including stakeholder consultation, before implementation.
The petitioner also raised concerns over voluntary compliance and the treatment of products already manufactured and supplied to retailers. The court sought clarity on how the transition would work once the final framework comes into force.
Another key issue was the treatment of added
sugar
. The petitioner questioned the FSSAI’s decision to focus on added sugar, pointing to an earlier position taken during the regulatory process.
The regulator, however, maintained that the distinction between naturally occurring sugar and sugar added during processing is important because consumers should know when sugar has been added to a product.
Packaged consumer goods companies will closely watch the outcome because the final framework could determine when manufacturers must alter packaging, how existing stock is treated, and what compliance steps will be required across their product portfolios.
Also Read
|
How Supreme Court's 13 questions to FSSAI could shape front-of-pack food labels
Legal disputes
Many companies have already challenged the FSSAI’s actions over misleading labels and packaging.
Before the Bombay high court, the regulator has argued that Old Monk cannot be sold simply as “rum” because of its composition and use of rum flavouring, and has sought changes to its labelling. Its maker has submitted revised labels to the court.
Dabur has challenged the FSSAI action over “100%” claims on products, including honey, ghee, and edible oils, before the Delhi high court.

The FSSAI had told the Court that further research was necessary to establish the precise health effects of microplastics, including the quantities that the human body could tolerate.
The Court directed that plastic or PET bottles containing drinking water carry the declaration “This water may contain Micro/Nano Plastics”. The warning was to appear in bold red letters, in a font size of at least 10.
Packaged sugar and salt were similarly required to carry the statement “This Sugar/Salt may contain Micro/Nano Plastics”.
The FSSAI was directed to notify the relevant manufacturers within four weeks of receiving the order uploaded on the court website and ensure compliance with the labelling requirements.
Why did FSSAI and industry associations seek a recall?
The FSSAI, the PET Packaging Association for Clean Environment (PACE) and the Federation of All India Packaged Drinking Water Manufacturers Associations sought reconsideration of the interim direction.
Their principal argument was that mandatory warnings were premature and disproportionate because scientific research had not conclusively established the harmful effects of microplastics at the levels detected in food and drinking water.
The FSSAI argued that the regulator needed to complete further studies before deciding whether additional labelling was warranted. It also maintained that regulatory measures should be evidence-based and proportionate, taking into account possible consumer panic, disruption to supply chains and the interests of food businesses.
Another concern was that the particles found in packaged water might have originated from the water source or environmental contamination, rather than exclusively from PET bottles.
PACE relied on existing Bureau of Indian Standards requirements governing packaging materials, including migration tests and prescribed limits. It also cited the World Health Organization’s report on microplastics in drinking water, arguing that the available evidence did not establish a human health concern.
The manufacturers’ associations further contended that the products complied with existing packaging and labelling regulations, which did not specifically require disclosures about microplastics. They argued that the Court should allow the FSSAI to discharge its statutory responsibilities and frame appropriate regulations.
Why did the Court reject these arguments?
The Bench said the interim order did not declare bottled water, sugar or salt to be unsafe. It required only disclosure of the possible presence of microplastics while further scientific studies continued.

New Delhi, The Supreme Court on Monday questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India over its proposed timeline for implementation of front-of-package labelling on packaged foods and asked why it wants to waste so much time when the matter relates to the health of citizens.
SC questions FSSAI over its proposed timeline for implementation of front-of-package labelling
Front-of-package labelling is a nutritional information graphic on food packaging that can assist consumers in making an informed decision about food purchases and healthier dietary choices.
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said why does FSSAI want to waste so much time when the matter relates to the health issue of the citizens.
"We appreciate whatever you have done so far and we appreciate your initiative but there is a lot which is required to be done to give meaningful effect to what we want to achieve and where we want to reach. We are undertaking this entire exercise for the good of the nation and for the good of the citizens. We expect the authority to accept our order in its true spirit.
"Why voluntary compliance for a year? Why do you need so much time? Why do you want to start afresh with the exercise of hearing and calling for objections? You started in 2022 what did you do in the last four years," the bench remarked while reserving its order in the matter.
The counsel for FSSAI told the court that what was initiated in 2022 was Indian Nutrition Rating star-rating system in 2022 and the yardstick was completely different then.
The FSSAI has now proposed adopting a red hexagonal warning label for packaged food products high in nutrients of concern such as sugar, fat and salt and it would use a red hexagon against a white square-shaped background on the front of food packages.
The food regulator told the top court that it would require approximately four months to issue and finalise the draft regulations.
It told the apex court that the draft amendment regulations would be published for 60 days to invite comments from stakeholders through domestic consultation and the WTO platform.
Further, FSSAI has proposed a 365-day voluntary implementation period for food business operators after notification of the regulations.
The top court had earlier asked the FSSAI, which has proposed phased implementation of front-of-package labelling on packaged foods, to come up with more clarifications on the planned labels of "nutrients of concern", fat, sugar and salt.
The apex court was hearing a plea of the public charitable trust '3S and Our Health Society' which sought directions to the Centre, states and Union territories to implement mandatory FoPL on packaged foods.
The FSSAI had earlier told the top court that it proposed to provide a prominent front-of-pack warning label in red for food products high in added saturated fat, added sugar and salt.
In a compliance affidavit filed last month, the FSSAI said the two-phased proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern.
The FSSAI's affidavit stated that the FoPL is intended to be implemented in phases to facilitate both "consumer acceptability" and "provide the industry adequate time for reformulation".
